analysis.one_liner: Raises civil penalties up to five-fold for oil, gas, and mining companies that violate federal leasing rules.
analysis.headline: A Democratic congresswoman and 19 Democratic cosponsors introduced the bill in September 2026; it was sent to two House committees, where no hearings or votes have taken place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises the maximum fines that companies operating on federal lands and offshore waters must pay when they violate leasing, safety, royalty, and pollution rules. It multiplies most existing penalty caps several times and adds automatic annual increases to keep fines from eroding with inflation. It also creates a fund that splits money from the new penalties between communities harmed by violations and the federal offices that enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near federal oil, gas, and mineral operations, including coastal communities and Tribal lands, get stronger financial deterrence against violations. States, Tribes, and local governments harmed by a violation would receive half of the penalty money above what old law allowed. Taxpayers also benefit because violators would repay more of the damage and lost royalties they cause.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near federal drilling and mining sites

how_it_helps.text: Raises the maximum daily penalty under the Mineral Leasing Act from $500,000 to $2,700,000 and a related penalty from $100,000 to $500,000, and adds an automatic annual inflation adjustment [S2].
Raises penalty caps under the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act roughly five-fold, for example from $50,000 to $320,000 for the most serious class, with annual inflation adjustment [S2].

Raises offshore penalties under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, including a new $360,000-per-day cap when a violation threatens life, property, or the marine environment, and increases another cap from $100,000 to $1,000,000 [S2].

Raises the Oil Pollution Act penalty from $25,000 to $120,000 and creates a Penalty Revenue Reinvestment Fund that directs half of excess penalty collections to States, Indian Tribes, and local governments harmed by the violation and half to federal enforcement offices [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and mineral companies operating under federal leases and offshore permits, which would face up to several times higher fines for violations. Some of that cost could be passed through to consumers in energy prices, though the penalties apply only to companies that violate the rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal-lease oil, gas, and mining operators

drawbacks.text: The higher penalties apply only to operations on federal lands and offshore waters, so pollution from comparable activity on state or private land is not covered [S2].

Opponents of higher fines generally argue they raise operating costs that can be passed to consumers and make smaller operators less able to compete against large companies; the bill's annual inflation indexing also makes the penalty amounts rise indefinitely [S2].
The new reinvestment fund only pays out when penalties above the old caps are actually assessed and collected, so its benefit to communities depends entirely on future enforcement actions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill strengthens a real but narrow deterrent: fines for violations of federal mineral and offshore leasing rules, which had not kept pace with either inflation or industry scale. The cost falls on companies that violate the rules, with some possible pass-through to energy prices. The main design limits are its coverage gap (federal operations only) and the fact that community payments depend on penalties actually being collected. As written it is a targeted increase in polluter liability, not a broad pollution-control measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees in September 2026, and with the session ending in early January 2027 no committee has taken it up.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 3, 2026, with 19 Democratic cosponsors, and referred to both the Natural Resources Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee [S1][S3][S4].
The only recorded action after introduction is the committee referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history [S4].
The 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027, and any bill not passed by then dies and must be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal oil, gas, and mineral operators, which have not faced the higher fines; a bill increasing their liability has advanced no further than committee referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal-lease oil, gas, and mineral operators

for.name: Rep. Maxine Dexter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill raising federal mineral and offshore penalties and created the penalty reinvestment fund.

for.name: 19 House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors including Reps. Bonamici, Huffman, Tonko, Norton, Cohen, and Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill a 20-member all-Democratic starting bloc.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 3, 2026, and has taken no further recorded action on the bill.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 3, 2026, and has taken no further recorded action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican signed on, and no committee action has occurred.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and mineral companies on federal leases and offshore waters
industries.note: The bill multiplies the fines these companies face for violating leasing, royalty, safety, and pollution rules several times over and indexes them to inflation. Their interest in avoiding the higher fines runs against the communities and taxpayers who bear the cost of violations.

industries.industry: Federal and state environmental enforcement agencies (ONRR, BSEE, BLM)
industries.note: Half of new excess penalty collections would fund the enforcement offices without needing annual appropriations, giving them a steadier budget for inspections and compliance work.

industries.industry: States, Tribes, and local governments near federal mineral operations
industries.note: They would receive half of collected penalty amounts above the old caps when a violation harms them, money they currently do not receive.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in two committees with no hearings, markup, or vote scheduled, all-Democratic sponsorship in a House controlled by Republicans, and only a few months left in the session. The realistic path is that it dies at the end of this Congress and would need to be reintroduced in the next one; the only other route to a floor vote, a procedure where a majority can force a bill out of committee, is rarely used and would need far more support than this bill has.
